name: Example: Solving a Differential Equation Using Variation of Parameters
problem:
$$
y''' + 4y'  =  6,  \qquad \big\{ y_1 = 1, \: y_2 = \cos(2x), \: y_3 = \sin(2x) \big\}
$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
y(x) = A + B \cos(2x) + C \sin(2x) + u_1(x) + u_2(x) \cos(2x) + u_3(x) \sin(2x).
$$

What is the function $u_3(x)?$
worked_solution:
According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y_p} = {u_1}{y_1} + {u_2}{y_2} + {u_3}{y_3},
\qquad
{u_i} = (-1)^{3-i} \int \frac{g(x){W_i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x, 
\qquad
i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of $y_1,y_2,y_3,$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{2}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{3}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x) = 6.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
y_1= 1, \qquad y_2= \cos(2x), \qquad y_3= \sin(2x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions $y_1,$ $y_2,$ and $y_3$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ 0 & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ 0 & -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & =8{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+8{cos}^{2}⁡(2x) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions $y_1,$ $y_2,$ and $y_3$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find $u_3,$ we compute the determinant $W_3(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{3}(x) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\ 0 & -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3}(x) & =(-1)^{3-3}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{3}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{6(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$
